package.title: Slowing AI Could Speed Up the Economy
package.promised: I expect an argument that deliberately slowing AI adoption or development could produce a healthier, faster-growing economy by keeping people employed and in the loop. The Trump/Uncle Sam image suggests it may frame this as a political or U.S. policy question about AI still needing human workers.

new_things: Trump wants America to win the AI race.
Anthropic’s Dario Amodei wants AI development to slow down.
The video suggests progress may come from fixing existing AI systems rather than simply moving faster.
AI can produce work that looks finished within seconds.
reports.held_question: What do you find after the AI-generated work first appears finished, and how does fixing it relate to moving AI forward?

new_things: AI can produce work with wrong numbers, missing sources, or unsaved files.
A job that appears finished can still require substantial manual cleanup.
Even if each step succeeds 19 times out of 20, chaining 20 steps means only about four jobs out of ten succeed.
reports.held_question: Why does chaining seemingly reliable AI steps make so many whole jobs fail?

new_things: A 20-step AI job with each step working 95% of the time finishes without mistakes only about four times out of ten.
If each step works 99% of the time, about eight out of ten such jobs finish cleanly.
Improving reliability could roughly double completed jobs for the same ten waiting customers.
The speaker sees that reliability improvement as an economic opportunity.
reports.held_question: How can AI systems be made reliable enough that more multi-step jobs finish cleanly?

new_things: More reliable automation would let a shop owner send a quote and move on to the next customer.
It would let an accountant finish a return instead of searching through made-up receipts.
Recovered hours across many businesses make reliability seem economically valuable.
reports.held_question: What larger economic opportunity does that reliability create?

new_things: Amodei’s argument is about safety, including improved testing and operations.
The speaker thinks that safety work could also create a productivity benefit.
A stronger model might make fewer mistakes.
The speaker is going to compare both approaches on the same job.
reports.held_question: How will the two approaches perform when they are put on the same job?
could_not_follow: Who Amodei is and what specific argument is being referenced.

new_things: The suggested test is to count how often people have to step in and fix AI.
Making current AI need less human fixing could save enough time that slowing frontier progress speeds up the economy.
The speaker says winning the AI race should give people their afternoons back.
reports.held_question: Would making today’s AI more reliable actually save more time than pushing quickly toward stronger models?
reports.asked_of_me: Count how often I have to step in.
